newsitem.title: UK: Reuters profit down, plans stock buyback.
newsitem.headline: Reuters profit down, plans stock buyback.

text.p: Global news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc, reporting a 3 percent drop in first-half profits due to the strong pound, said Wednesday it planned to repurchase shares worth up to 200 million pounds ($335.8 million).

Pre-tax profit in the six months ended June 30 fell to 333 million pounds ($560 million) from 342 million ($575 million) a year earlier, the company said. However, profits were 12 percent higher when measured at comparable exchange rates.
The company generates more than 80 percent of its income overseas.

Revenue fell 29 million pounds ($48.7 million) to 1.41 billion ($2.37 billion) but rose by 8 percent at comparable exchange rates. Reuters said underlying margins were maintained despite the cost of rolling out its new 3000 product range.
Chief Executive Peter Job said underlying revenue growth was expected to remain around the 8 percent level for 1997 as a whole.

The profit figure was near the bottom of analysts' forecasts and Reuters shares fell 14.5p to 595p, giving up earlier gains. In early Nasdaq trading, its American Depositary Receipts lost $2.375 to $59.875.

Analysts and dealers said the results did not provide enough of a positive surprise to allow the stock to build on a recent rally. "The numbers are all right but the fact that they (profits) are down and they are only distributing 200 million has disappointed the market," said NatWest analyst Neill Junor.
The interim dividend was raised by 13 percent to 3.1 pence. Reuters said it expected to maintain double-digit dividend growth in 1997.
Job said the buy-back sum, which will offset growth in the company's 1.12 billion pounds cash mountain, was the maximum it could return to shareholders efficiently under British tax rules.
"If you go beyond a certain limit you simply get involved in unrecoverable tax, which is not very good for shareholders," Job said in an interview.
Job said the recent British budget resulted in a more level playing field for shareholders in relation to share buybacks, although advance corporation tax, or ACT, remained a major constraint.

He said the company would carry out a share repurchase programme "to return up to 200 million, which is possible within our ACT constraints. We continue to review developments in this area in relation to a more substantial return of cash."
The company was forced last October to scrap plans to return 613 million pounds ($1.03 billion) to shareholders after the previous government changed the tax rules.
Job said Reuters would continue to seek a way through what he termed a "maze of tax and other regulations" to return more of its cash surplus to shareholders.

The company said it believed the British system should be brought in line with that in the United States to allow companies to acquire their own shares in a tax neutral manner without having to cancel them.

Reuters forecast a slight decline in profit margins over the next two years as it gears up for European monetary union and the new millennium. Job said the millennium would be an opportunity to phase out obsolete products and identified the Internet as a potential growth area.

The company said the return of 200 million pounds over the next 12 months would offset the growth in cash balances. Net funds increased by 71 million pounds ($119 million) to 1.12 billion ($1.88 billion) in the first half.
The company said it did not expect the strong pound to impact its marketing positioning adversely, but currency factors were likely to continue to restrict revenue and earnings.
Reuters said revenue from its information products business grew by 7 percent from a year earlier at comparable exchange rates. Market share also improved.
Installations of the 3000 series, slow to begin, picked up strongly, with 10,600 installed and orders now totalling 24,300.
Transaction products revenue grew by 10 percent at comparable rates, with revenue at Instinet, the electronic equity brokerage, ahead by 17 percent.
Revenue from the Dealing 2000 foreign exchange products rose by 4 percent at comparable rates.
